title: Previous papers (collected)
des: Oman Pearson VUE paediatrics questions collected from several earlier candidates' papers (Dr Heba, Dr Huda, Dr Mai and others, from 2016). Answers checked and explained.

questions.question: A child with sickle cell disease has an acute stroke. Below what level should transfusion bring the HbS percentage?
questions.exp: Exchange transfusion for acute stroke (and chronic transfusion to prevent recurrence) aims to keep HbS below 30% while keeping total Hb around 10 g/dL to avoid hyperviscosity.

questions.question: A child swallowed a coin and has no choking or respiratory distress. The X-ray shows the coin in the distal oesophagus at the lower oesophageal sphincter. What should be done?
questions.d: Repeat the X-ray within 12–24 hours; remove endoscopically if it has not passed into the stomach
questions.e: Give milk and discharge without follow-up
questions.exp: Asymptomatic coins in the distal oesophagus often pass into the stomach within hours, so observation with a repeat X-ray (within 24 hours) is reasonable. Remove if still there, or immediately if symptomatic (drooling, distress). Button batteries in the oesophagus are always an emergency.

questions.question: What is the first-line treatment of idiopathic nephrotic syndrome in a child?
questions.exp: First presentation: prednisolone 60 mg/m²/day (max 60 mg) for 4 weeks, then 40 mg/m² on alternate days for 4 weeks. Most children (minimal change) respond. Ciclosporin, tacrolimus, cyclophosphamide, MMF or rituximab are for frequently relapsing, steroid-dependent or resistant disease.

questions.question: A girl has sudden abdominal pain 3 weeks after an upper respiratory infection. The surgeons have excluded appendicitis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Mesenteric adenitis (inflamed mesenteric lymph nodes after a viral infection) mimics appendicitis with right lower quadrant pain and fever; ultrasound shows enlarged nodes and a normal appendix. It resolves with supportive care.

questions.question: A child with bronchopulmonary dysplasia on diuretics has a blood gas of pH 7.54, HCO3 23 mmol/L and pCO2 4.7 kPa. What is the acid–base disorder?
questions.exp: pH is high (alkalaemia). pCO2 of 4.7 kPa (35 mmHg) is at the low end of normal and bicarbonate is normal, so with these numbers the change is respiratory. In practice, chronic diuretic use in BPD more often causes a metabolic alkalosis (contraction, hypochloraemia), so check chloride and potassium.

questions.question: A child has faecal and urinary incontinence without trauma, and 2 previous urinary infections. What is the investigation?
questions.a: Plain X-ray of the abdomen only
questions.exp: New bladder and bowel dysfunction suggests a neurogenic cause: tethered cord, occult spinal dysraphism (look for a sacral dimple, hair tuft or lipoma), spinal tumour or transverse myelitis. MRI of the spine is the key test; urodynamics follows.

questions.question: A child has difficulty passing stool, eats junk food and does little exercise. Stools are hard and infrequent. What is the treatment?
questions.b: A stool softener (macrogol) with dietary and toileting advice
questions.exp: NICE: functional constipation is treated first with an osmotic laxative (polyethylene glycol), disimpaction if needed, then maintenance for months, together with fluids, fibre, activity and regular toileting. Diet alone is not enough as first-line treatment.

questions.question: A child with lower abdominal pain and irritability has a urinalysis with white cells over 10 and red cells over 10 per field. What is the treatment?
questions.b: Antibiotics for urinary tract infection (after sending a culture)
questions.exp: Pyuria and haematuria with lower abdominal pain suggest cystitis; send a urine culture and start empirical antibiotics, adjusting to sensitivities.

questions.question: What is the commonest site of intussusception in children?
questions.exp: Most childhood intussusceptions are ileocolic, from lymphoid hyperplasia (Peyer's patches) after viral infection, at 6–36 months. Small-bowel intussusceptions are often transient; lead points (Meckel, polyp, lymphoma, HSP) are more likely in older children.

questions.question: A 2-day-old has a red rash with small white or yellow papules on a red base on the face and trunk; a smear shows eosinophils. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Erythema toxicum is a benign rash in the first days of life: blotchy erythema with papules and pustules containing eosinophils, fading within 1–2 weeks. Bacterial pustules contain neutrophils and need antibiotics.

questions.question: A newborn has a soft mass protruding from one side of the nose that gets bigger when crying. Which investigation excludes intracranial connection?
questions.exp: A nasal mass that enlarges with crying or compression of the jugular veins (positive Furstenberg test) suggests an encephalocele (or a nasal glioma or dermoid). MRI shows any connection to the brain; never biopsy before imaging because of CSF leak and meningitis risk.

questions.question: A 9-month-old with a cold develops respiratory distress and wheeze, with one short cyanotic episode. What is the commonest organism?
questions.exp: Bronchiolitis (RSV most commonly) affects infants under 1 year: coryza, then cough, tachypnoea, recession, crackles and wheeze; young infants can have apnoeas. Management is supportive. Parainfluenza causes croup.

questions.question: What is first-line treatment for mild acne in an adolescent?
questions.e: Topical benzoyl peroxide (with or without a topical retinoid)
questions.exp: Mild to moderate acne: topical benzoyl peroxide and/or a topical retinoid (adapalene), or fixed combinations with clindamycin. Oral antibiotics (doxycycline) for moderate inflammatory acne, combined with topical treatment; isotretinoin for severe or scarring acne.

questions.question: A child with tetralogy of Fallot has frequent cyanotic spells while awaiting surgery. What can prevent them?
questions.exp: Beta-blockers relax the infundibular spasm and reduce spells until surgical repair. Digoxin and diuretics are avoided. Prostaglandin is for duct-dependent newborns.

questions.question: A child took a large iron overdose and had only diarrhoea after 6 hours, then seemed better. What may happen if he is not treated?
questions.exp: Iron poisoning stages: GI (vomiting, bloody diarrhoea, 0–6 h), a latent phase (6–24 h) that can falsely reassure, then shock and metabolic acidosis, hepatic necrosis (2–3 days) and later gastric outlet stricture. Treat significant levels or symptoms with IV desferrioxamine.

questions.question: Which test helps tell infectious mononucleosis caused by EBV from a CMV mononucleosis-like illness?
questions.b: Heterophile antibody (Monospot) test, positive in EBV
questions.exp: Heterophile antibodies are produced in EBV infection (positive in most teenagers, often negative in young children) but not in CMV, which causes a heterophile-negative mononucleosis. EBV VCA IgM and CMV IgM confirm.

questions.question: Which drug can be used for migraine prophylaxis in a child?
questions.exp: Prophylaxis is considered for frequent or disabling migraine: propranolol (not in asthma), topiramate, amitriptyline, pizotifen or flunarizine. Ibuprofen, paracetamol and triptans treat attacks.

questions.question: A child has a severe headache with vomiting on waking. He is now sleepy with a GCS of 10. What should be done?
questions.d: Urgent CT scan of the brain
questions.exp: Early morning headache with vomiting and a falling conscious level suggest raised intracranial pressure (tumour, hydrocephalus, haemorrhage). Protect the airway and get urgent neuroimaging; lumbar puncture is contraindicated until a mass is excluded.

questions.question: A child had right-sided facial and limb jerking for 2 minutes, recurring 3 times in a week. Blood tests are normal. What should be done?
questions.d: EEG, followed by MRI brain for focal seizures
questions.exp: Recurrent unprovoked seizures need an EEG; focal seizures (unless typical of self-limited childhood epilepsies) also need an MRI brain to look for a structural cause.

questions.question: A child has Sturge–Weber syndrome. What should be screened for regularly?
questions.exp: Glaucoma affects up to 60% of children with a port-wine stain involving the upper eyelid (ophthalmic division); check intraocular pressure regularly from birth.

questions.question: Which is a vitamin K-dependent factor?
questions.exp: Vitamin K is needed for factors II, VII, IX and X, and proteins C and S (anticoagulants). Antithrombin, factor XI, XII and VIII are not vitamin K dependent.

questions.question: A toddler has bow legs (genu varum). Growth and examination are otherwise normal. What should be done?
questions.a: Reassure; physiological bowing resolves by about 2–3 years
questions.exp: Physiological genu varum is normal until about 18–24 months, then legs become straight and later knock-kneed (peak at 3–4 years). Investigate if severe, asymmetric, progressive after 2 years, or with short stature (rickets, Blount disease, skeletal dysplasia).

questions.question: What is the sodium concentration of 3% sodium chloride?
questions.exp: 0.9% saline has 154 mmol/L sodium, 0.45% has 77 mmol/L, and 3% has about 513 mmol/L (roughly 0.5 mmol/mL). 3% saline (2–5 mL/kg) is used for raised ICP or severe symptomatic hyponatraemia.

questions.question: What is the daily maintenance fluid requirement for a 25 kg child (Holliday–Segar)?
questions.exp: 100 mL/kg for the first 10 kg (1000) + 50 mL/kg for the next 10 kg (500) + 20 mL/kg above 20 kg (100) = 1600 mL a day (about 65 mL/hour). Use isotonic fluids with glucose, and restrict in conditions with high ADH.

questions.question: A child has a dystonia that is worse in the evening and improves after sleep (Segawa disease). What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Dopa-responsive dystonia (GCH1 mutation) typically starts with leg dystonia in childhood, with diurnal fluctuation, and responds dramatically and lastingly to low-dose levodopa. Give a levodopa trial in any child with unexplained dystonia.

questions.question: Which is a contraindication to lumbar puncture?
questions.c: Signs of raised intracranial pressure or brain herniation
questions.exp: Contraindications: signs of raised ICP or herniation (reduced or fluctuating consciousness, focal signs, papilloedema, abnormal posture or pupils, bradycardia with hypertension), shock, a skin infection at the site, coagulopathy or platelets under about 50, and recent seizures in some guidelines.

questions.question: How is the mid-parental height calculated for a boy?
questions.exp: Boys: (father + mother + 13 cm) / 2; girls: (father + mother − 13 cm) / 2. The target range is about ±8.5 cm.

questions.question: An infant with suspected shaken baby syndrome has focal seizures. What else is likely on examination?
questions.exp: Abusive head trauma: subdural haemorrhages, extensive multilayered retinal haemorrhages, encephalopathy, and often rib or metaphyseal fractures. All infants with suspected abuse need a dilated eye examination by an ophthalmologist.

questions.question: Which factors does cryoprecipitate contain?
questions.a: Fibrinogen, factor VIII, von Willebrand factor, factor XIII and fibronectin
questions.e: Factors II, VII, IX and X only
questions.exp: Cryoprecipitate is used mainly to replace fibrinogen (in DIC and massive bleeding); FFP contains all factors; prothrombin complex concentrate contains II, VII, IX and X.

questions.question: A child has recurrent headaches with vomiting and abdominal pain, with complete recovery between attacks and a family history. What type of headache is it?
questions.exp: Childhood migraine: attacks often shorter and bilateral, with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, photophobia, and sleep relieving it. Abdominal migraine and cyclical vomiting are migraine equivalents.

questions.question: What is a suitable IV treatment for acute pyelonephritis in an ill infant?
questions.exp: For ill infants and children with pyelonephritis needing IV treatment: a third-generation cephalosporin (or gentamicin, or ampicillin plus gentamicin in young infants to cover Enterococcus), switching to oral once improving, for 7–10 days total. Amoxicillin resistance in E. coli is common; nitrofurantoin does not reach renal tissue.

questions.question: A baby follows an object to the midline but not past it. What is the likely age?
questions.exp: Visual following: to the midline at about 4–6 weeks, through 180 degrees by about 3 months. Social smile at 6 weeks.

questions.question: A child can copy a circle but not a square. What is the likely age?
questions.exp: Copies a vertical line at 2 years, a circle at 3, a cross at 3.5–4, a square at 4, a triangle at 5 and a diamond at 6.

questions.question: After a bicycle handlebar injury with pancreatitis, a child returns 2 weeks later with an epigastric mass and raised lipase. What is the next investigation?
questions.e: Abdominal ultrasound or CT to look for a pancreatic pseudocyst
questions.exp: A pancreatic pseudocyst forms 2–4 weeks after pancreatitis or trauma: epigastric mass, pain, persistent raised enzymes. Ultrasound or CT confirms; most resolve, while large or symptomatic ones are drained.

questions.question: A girl had a tonic–clonic seizure after being frightened in a fight with her brother and recovered fully before reaching hospital. What should be done?
questions.exp: After a first unprovoked seizure with full recovery and a normal neurological examination, emergency imaging is not needed; arrange an EEG and specialist review. Emotional triggers can also cause syncope or reflex anoxic seizures, so take a careful eyewitness history.

questions.question: A parent refuses MMR because they fear it causes autism. What should be advised?
questions.a: Deny all care until they agree
questions.d: Explain that research shows no link between vaccines and autism and recommend vaccination
questions.exp: Large studies have found no link between MMR and autism; the original paper was fraudulent and retracted. Listen to concerns, give clear evidence, and recommend vaccination; respect parental decision-making while documenting the discussion.

questions.question: A young child with fever and cough has a well-defined round opacity on the chest X-ray. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Round pneumonia is common under 8 years (poorly developed collateral air passages), usually pneumococcal. Treat with antibiotics and repeat the X-ray; image further (CT) only if it does not resolve or features are atypical.

questions.question: Two parents are carriers of an autosomal recessive disease, and one daughter is affected. What is the chance that the next child is affected?
questions.exp: Each pregnancy of two carriers has a 25% risk of an affected child, independent of previous children. An unaffected sibling has a 2/3 chance of being a carrier.

questions.question: A child has acute asymmetrical flaccid paralysis with fever and no sensory loss. What should be suspected?
questions.e: Poliomyelitis (or another enterovirus such as EV-D68)
questions.exp: Acute flaccid paralysis that is asymmetric, with fever, meningism and preserved sensation, suggests anterior horn cell infection: poliovirus or non-polio enteroviruses (acute flaccid myelitis). Send stool samples for polio surveillance. Guillain–Barré is symmetrical and ascending.

questions.question: A baby with hypoglycaemia has a physiological counter-regulatory response. Which hormone rises?
questions.exp: Hypoglycaemia normally suppresses insulin and raises glucagon, adrenaline, cortisol and growth hormone. Hypoglycaemia with detectable insulin suggests hyperinsulinism; low cortisol or GH suggests hypopituitarism.

questions.question: A child from a malaria-endemic area has fever, myalgia, anaemia and low platelets. What is the best investigation?
questions.b: Thick and thin blood films (Giemsa) for malaria
questions.exp: Falciparum malaria causes fever, anaemia, thrombocytopenia, splenomegaly and cerebral malaria. Repeat films 12–24 hours apart (3 times) if negative; rapid antigen tests help.

questions.question: What is the first sign of puberty in girls?
questions.exp: Thelarche at 8–13 years is usually first, then pubic hair, the growth spurt, and menarche about 2–2.5 years after thelarche. In boys, testicular enlargement (4 mL) is first.

questions.question: A child swallowed a detergent (cleanser). He is drooling and refuses to swallow. What should be done?
questions.e: Discharge if there are no mouth burns
questions.exp: Corrosive ingestion with drooling, dysphagia or vomiting needs endoscopy to assess oesophageal burns. Do not induce vomiting or neutralise.

questions.question: A cyanosed newborn needed prostaglandin E1 and a balloon atrial septostomy. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: TGA with intact ventricular septum needs mixing: prostaglandin keeps the duct open and balloon atrial septostomy (Rashkind) opens the atrial communication, before the arterial switch operation in the first 2–3 weeks.

questions.question: What is the commonest congenital anomaly of the small intestine?
questions.exp: Meckel diverticulum (a remnant of the vitellointestinal duct) is present in about 2% of people; most are symptomless, but it can cause painless rectal bleeding, intussusception, obstruction or diverticulitis.

questions.question: A child with iron deficiency anaemia starts oral iron. What is the first sign of response?
questions.exp: Reticulocytes rise within 5–10 days, haemoglobin rises about 1–2 g/dL per week, and iron stores take months; continue iron for 3 months after Hb normalises.

questions.question: What is the commonest cause of congenital hypothyroidism?
questions.a: Thyroid dysgenesis (agenesis, hypoplasia or ectopic gland)
questions.exp: Dysgenesis accounts for about 80% (mostly ectopic thyroid), dyshormonogenesis for 10–15%. Newborn screening (raised TSH) allows thyroxine treatment within 2 weeks, preventing intellectual disability.

questions.question: A child has diplopia when looking to the left. The left eye cannot abduct. Which nerve is affected?
questions.exp: The abducens nerve supplies lateral rectus. A left VI palsy causes horizontal diplopia worse on looking left. In children, a new VI palsy can be a false localising sign of raised ICP, so check for papilloedema and image.

questions.question: A child has hypoglycaemia and hepatomegaly. Which enzyme deficiency is most likely?
questions.exp: GSD I: fasting hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis, hyperlipidaemia and hyperuricaemia, from glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency.

questions.question: Which congenital heart lesion most often leads to pulmonary hypertension?
questions.exp: Large post-tricuspid shunts (VSD, PDA, AVSD) expose the lungs to high pressure and flow, causing early pulmonary vascular disease and Eisenmenger syndrome if not closed within the first year or two. ASDs cause pulmonary hypertension rarely and late.

questions.question: A baby is born to a hepatitis B surface antigen-positive mother. What should he receive?
questions.e: Hepatitis B immunoglobulin and hepatitis B vaccine within 12 hours of birth
questions.exp: HBIG plus vaccine at birth, completing the course, prevents over 90% of transmission.

questions.question: A child snores with apnoeic pauses during sleep but is otherwise normal. Which test confirms obstructive sleep apnoea?
questions.exp: Overnight polysomnography is the gold standard for OSA; overnight oximetry can support it. Adenotonsillectomy is the main treatment.

questions.question: What is the treatment of Wilson disease?
questions.d: D-penicillamine (or trientine), with zinc for maintenance
questions.exp: Wilson disease (ATP7B): low caeruloplasmin, high urine copper, Kayser–Fleischer rings, liver disease and later neuropsychiatric features. Chelation with penicillamine or trientine; zinc reduces copper absorption; low-copper diet; transplant for acute liver failure.

questions.question: A child has a metabolic acidosis (pH 7.3) with a normal anion gap and high chloride. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic) acidosis comes from bicarbonate loss through the gut (diarrhoea) or kidney (RTA). High anion gap causes include ketoacidosis, lactate, toxins and renal failure. The urine anion gap helps separate gut from renal loss.

questions.question: A child after trauma has a heart rate of 160, respiratory rate 40, normal temperature and normal blood pressure, with bruises over the body. What type of shock is this?
questions.exp: Tachycardia and tachypnoea with a normal BP after trauma = compensated haemorrhagic shock; hypotension comes late. Give fluid or blood boluses and find the bleeding.

questions.question: A child has suspected septic arthritis. What is the key investigation?
questions.d: Joint aspiration (with Gram stain and culture)
questions.exp: Aspiration (usually ultrasound-guided, often in theatre with washout) confirms the diagnosis and organism; take blood cultures first and start IV antibiotics after samples. Staphylococcus aureus and Kingella kingae (under 4 years) are commonest.

questions.question: Which fluid is used first to treat dehydration with shock?
questions.exp: Use isotonic crystalloid boluses (10 mL/kg, reassess, repeat). Colloids have no benefit and dextrose-only fluids cause hyponatraemia.

questions.question: A 5-year-old girl has vaginal bleeding, bruising and itching. What should be considered first?
questions.b: Sexual abuse (with testing for gonorrhoea and other STIs)
questions.exp: Genital bruising and bleeding in a prepubertal girl are highly concerning for sexual abuse; a sexually transmitted infection (gonorrhoea, chlamydia, trichomonas, syphilis) beyond the newborn period is strong evidence. Refer to child protection; examination by an expert. Consider foreign body, lichen sclerosus, urethral prolapse and precocious puberty.

questions.question: An infant has weakness and hypotonia. Which first test helps tell muscle disease from other causes?
questions.exp: A high CK suggests muscular dystrophy or myopathy; a normal CK with fasciculations suggests SMA (confirm with SMN1 genetic test). Most floppy infants have a central cause (brain), with weakness less prominent than hypotonia.

questions.question: Which vaccine is given subcutaneously?
questions.exp: MMR and varicella are live vaccines traditionally given subcutaneously (IM is also acceptable for MMR). Inactivated adjuvanted vaccines (DTaP, Hib, hepatitis B, PCV) are given IM to reduce local reactions.

questions.question: By what age are all 20 primary teeth usually present?
questions.exp: Primary teeth erupt from about 6 months (lower central incisors) and the second molars come in by 2–3 years. Permanent teeth begin at about 6 years with first molars and lower incisors.

questions.question: A newborn drools excessively and coughs and chokes with the first feed; a nasogastric tube cannot be passed, and the abdomen is soft. Meconium was passed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.c: Oesophageal atresia with a distal tracheo-oesophageal fistula
questions.exp: The commonest type (about 85%) is atresia with a distal fistula: drooling, choking with feeds, and a tube that coils in the upper pouch on X-ray, with air in the stomach. Isolated atresia gives a gasless abdomen. H-type fistula presents later with recurrent chest infections. Look for VACTERL anomalies.

questions.question: A child has a week of thigh pain with a tender mass. X-ray shows a lesion in the metaphysis with sunburst periosteal reaction and a Codman triangle. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Osteosarcoma: adolescents, metaphysis of long bones around the knee, sunburst and Codman triangle. Ewing sarcoma: diaphysis or flat bones, onion-skin periosteal reaction, systemic symptoms, t(11;22).

questions.question: A boy has precocious puberty, and CT shows a pineal region tumour. What is the most likely type?
questions.exp: Pineal and suprasellar germ cell tumours (germinomas and non-germinomatous) secrete hCG and cause precocious puberty in boys; they may also cause Parinaud syndrome and diabetes insipidus. Check serum and CSF hCG and AFP.

questions.question: Which enzyme is deficient in classic galactosaemia?
questions.exp: Classic galactosaemia (GALT) causes vomiting, jaundice, liver failure, cataracts and E. coli sepsis after milk feeds. Galactokinase deficiency causes cataracts only; aldolase B deficiency is hereditary fructose intolerance.

questions.question: A breastfed baby loses 7% of his birth weight in the first week but feeds well and is otherwise well. What should be done?
questions.e: Reassure, support breastfeeding and recheck the weight
questions.exp: Up to 10% weight loss in the first week is normal; birth weight is usually regained by 2 weeks. Losses over 10% need a feeding assessment and checks for hypernatraemic dehydration and jaundice.

questions.question: Which antibiotic is a good choice for aspiration pneumonia?
questions.a: Co-amoxiclav (or clindamycin) to cover oral anaerobes
questions.exp: Community aspiration pneumonia is usually polymicrobial with oral anaerobes and streptococci; co-amoxiclav (amoxicillin–clavulanate) or clindamycin is suitable; add Gram-negative cover if hospital-acquired.

questions.question: A 12-year-old girl is 125 cm tall. Her father is 158 cm and mother 152 cm, and her bone age is 8 years. What is the most likely cause?
questions.b: Normal variant needing no further thought
questions.c: Familial short stature combined with constitutional delay
questions.exp: Both parents are short (familial short stature) and the bone age is delayed by 4 years (constitutional delay), which together explain short stature with a normal growth velocity. A delayed bone age with a LOW growth velocity would point to GH deficiency or hypothyroidism. A karyotype is still advised in short girls.

questions.question: A child with asthma took oral steroids for 1 week, followed by an inhaled steroid. Can he receive his 4–6-year live vaccines?
questions.exp: Live vaccines are delayed only after high-dose steroids (2 mg/kg/day or 20 mg/day or more) for 14 days or longer, until 1 month after stopping. A short course or inhaled steroids are not a contraindication.

questions.question: A child has progressive ascending weakness with loss of deep tendon reflexes. What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Guillain–Barré syndrome is treated with IVIG (2 g/kg) or plasma exchange if the child cannot walk or is deteriorating; steroids do not help. Monitor vital capacity, swallowing and autonomic instability.

questions.question: A well child at a routine visit has a middle ear effusion without symptoms. What should be done?
questions.b: Watchful waiting and review after about 3 months
questions.exp: Otitis media with effusion usually resolves within 3 months; review with a hearing test. Grommets are considered for bilateral effusion with hearing loss persisting over 3 months, or with speech or learning problems.

questions.question: A term baby born after prolonged rupture of membranes has tonic seizures of the right arm. Where is the haemorrhage most likely?
questions.e: Left frontal or parietal lobe (focal stroke or haemorrhage)
questions.exp: Focal seizures in a term neonate suggest a focal lesion on the opposite side (perinatal arterial ischaemic stroke or haemorrhage). IVH is mainly a preterm problem. Neonatal infection (from PROM) must be excluded too. MRI is the best test.

questions.question: A girl with an umbilical hernia is irritable with abdominal pain. Blood count is normal and the hernia is soft and reducible. What should be done?
questions.a: Reassure; most umbilical hernias close by 4–5 years
questions.exp: Umbilical hernias rarely incarcerate and usually close by 4–5 years; elective repair if persisting beyond then or very large. A tender, irreducible hernia needs urgent surgery. Look for another cause of abdominal pain.

questions.question: What is the most commonly aspirated foreign body in young children?
questions.exp: Food (especially nuts and seeds) is the commonest aspirated foreign body in toddlers; coins are commonly swallowed (oesophageal). Advise no whole nuts under 5 years.

questions.question: A child is convulsing and IV access is difficult. What should be given?
questions.d: Buccal or intranasal midazolam (or rectal diazepam)
questions.e: IV lorazepam after 30 minutes of trying
questions.exp: If there is no IV access, give buccal or intranasal midazolam (0.3 mg/kg) or rectal diazepam (0.5 mg/kg), then repeat or go to IO access.

questions.question: A child has eczema, recurrent infections and thrombocytopenia with small platelets. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Wiskott–Aldrich (X-linked): eczema, small platelets with bleeding, recurrent infections, autoimmunity and lymphoma risk.

questions.question: Where do B lymphocytes mature?
questions.exp: B cells develop in the bone marrow; T cells mature in the thymus. Plasma cells (antibody production) form in lymph nodes and spleen after antigen exposure.

questions.question: A 3-day-old has hypoglycaemia with a seizure. What is the treatment?
questions.c: 2 mL/kg 10% dextrose bolus, followed by a glucose infusion (about 6–8 mg/kg/min)
questions.exp: Symptomatic hypoglycaemia needs IV 10% dextrose bolus then infusion; high requirements suggest hyperinsulinism.

questions.question: Which electrolyte disturbance is typical of cystic fibrosis in infants?
questions.exp: Excessive salt loss in sweat can cause pseudo-Bartter syndrome in infants with CF, especially in hot weather.

questions.question: Which drug is NOT used during a tetralogy of Fallot hypercyanotic spell?
questions.exp: Inotropes such as digoxin increase infundibular contraction and worsen the spell. Use oxygen, knee-chest position, morphine, fluids, beta-blockers and phenylephrine.

questions.question: A child dies on the second day after a paracetamol overdose. What is the most likely cause of death?
questions.e: Cerebral oedema from acute liver failure
questions.exp: Paracetamol-induced acute liver failure peaks at 3–4 days with encephalopathy; cerebral oedema and herniation are the main causes of death, along with multiorgan failure and sepsis.

questions.question: A child with hypothyroidism has generalised muscle hypertrophy (pseudohypertrophy). What is the syndrome?
questions.exp: Kocher–Debré–Semelaigne syndrome: long-standing hypothyroidism with muscle pseudohypertrophy (Herculean look) and raised CK; it resolves with thyroxine. Pendred syndrome is goitre with deafness.

questions.question: A child has haematuria and a blood pressure of 150/90 with headache. What is the appropriate drug for a hypertensive emergency?
questions.exp: Hypertensive emergency (with symptoms such as headache, encephalopathy, seizures) needs a titratable IV drug: labetalol or nicardipine infusion (hydralazine bolus as an alternative), lowering BP by no more than 25% in the first 8 hours.

questions.question: A 14-year-old girl has poor school performance and a webbed neck. What is the investigation?
questions.exp: Webbed neck in a girl suggests Turner syndrome (or Noonan); a karyotype confirms Turner.

questions.question: Which drug is used to treat ADHD?
questions.exp: Methylphenidate (stimulant) is first-line medication from 5–6 years, alongside behavioural support; atomoxetine, guanfacine and lisdexamfetamine are alternatives.

questions.question: An 18-month-old uncircumcised boy has abdominal pain, irritability and dark, smelly urine. How should urine be collected for culture?
questions.exp: In infants who are not toilet-trained, a clean-catch sample is preferred; if not possible or the child is ill, use a catheter or suprapubic aspiration. Bag samples are often contaminated.

questions.question: An ECG shows ventricular tachycardia in a child with a pulse who is haemodynamically stable. What is the drug treatment?
questions.exp: Stable VT: amiodarone or procainamide after expert advice; unstable VT with a pulse: synchronised cardioversion; pulseless VT: defibrillation. Adenosine is for SVT and verapamil is avoided in children.

questions.question: A child cries whenever his mother leaves him at school or with a babysitter, and sleeps with his mother. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Separation anxiety disorder: excessive distress on separation from attachment figures, worry about harm, refusing school, sleeping away or alone, beyond what is normal for age (normal separation anxiety peaks at 9–18 months). Treat with CBT and parent work.

questions.question: A toxic child is drooling with suspected epiglottitis. What is the priority?
questions.b: Secure the airway (intubation by a senior anaesthetist), then antibiotics
questions.d: Examine the throat with a tongue depressor
questions.e: Lateral neck X-ray before anything else
questions.exp: Keep the child calm and upright, call senior anaesthesia and ENT, secure the airway in a controlled setting, then give IV ceftriaxone.

questions.question: A child chokes on peanuts and becomes unresponsive. Two rescue breaths do not work. What is the next step according to BLS?
questions.exp: An unresponsive choking child needs CPR: open the airway, look for and remove visible objects, 5 rescue breaths, then chest compressions without checking for signs of life; compressions help expel the object.

questions.question: A baby supports his head, sits with support and screams when someone takes his toy. What is his age?
questions.exp: At 6–9 months infants show stranger anxiety, protest when a toy is taken, and transfer objects. Head control is at 3–4 months.

questions.question: A newborn has meconium ileus, and his brother died of failure to thrive. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Meconium ileus affects 10–20% of babies with CF; do a sweat test (after 2 weeks and 2 kg) and CFTR genetics.

questions.question: A child has petechiae after a recent viral illness, suggesting ITP. What is the first investigation?
questions.a: Full blood count and blood film
questions.exp: ITP is diagnosed by isolated thrombocytopenia with an otherwise normal blood count and film. Bone marrow is only needed for atypical features (other cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, bone pain).

questions.question: A child with croup is cyanosed with severe stridor. What is the immediate treatment?
questions.e: Oxygen and nebulised adrenaline, plus dexamethasone
questions.exp: Severe croup: give oxygen, nebulised adrenaline (rapid but short effect), dexamethasone or budesonide, and senior help; prepare for intubation with a smaller tube if failing.

questions.question: A 6-month-old develops vomiting, diarrhoea and failure to thrive after fruit is added to his diet. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.exp: Hereditary fructose intolerance presents at weaning when fructose (fruit, sucrose) is introduced: vomiting, hypoglycaemia, liver and kidney dysfunction. Avoid fructose, sucrose and sorbitol.

questions.question: A 4-year-old keeps copying a superhero by jumping from heights and has had many injuries. What should the mother be advised?
questions.b: Supervise and modify what he watches, and talk with him about what is safe
questions.d: Let him watch only 5 hours a day
questions.exp: Young children imitate media and cannot tell fantasy from reality; parents should choose age-appropriate programmes, watch with the child, explain, and limit screen time to about 1 hour a day at 2–5 years.

questions.question: A child wants to let go of his mother's hand while crossing the road. What advice should be given?
questions.d: Avoid the situation where possible and keep holding his hand firmly, explaining road safety
questions.exp: Young children cannot judge traffic speed and distance until about 9–11 years; adults should always hold their hand near traffic and teach road safety by example. Harsh punishment is not recommended.

questions.question: An infant has heart failure and hydrocephalus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: A vein of Galen malformation causes high-output heart failure in newborns and hydrocephalus (venous hypertension, compression) in infants.

questions.question: What is the chance that a daughter of a man with haemophilia A is a carrier?
questions.exp: An affected father passes his X to all daughters (obligate carriers) and his Y to all sons (unaffected).

questions.question: An infant had anaphylaxis after the 4-month vaccines and is due for the 6-month vaccines. What is the advice?
questions.c: Refer to an allergist to identify the trigger before further doses
questions.exp: Anaphylaxis to a previous dose of a vaccine (or a component) is a contraindication to that vaccine until assessed by an allergist, who can identify the component and advise how to complete the schedule safely.

questions.question: Which vaccine is live attenuated?
questions.exp: Live vaccines: MMR, varicella, BCG, rotavirus, oral polio, yellow fever, live intranasal influenza.

questions.question: A child asks many questions, fights with her brother over the TV channel and paints her room pink. What age is most likely?
questions.exp: At 4 years, children ask "why" questions constantly, play imaginatively, argue and have strong preferences.

questions.question: What is the first-line management of developmental dysplasia of the hip in a young infant?
questions.exp: Unstable or dislocated hips under 6 months are treated with a Pavlik harness (abduction and flexion); closed reduction and spica if it fails or after 6 months.

questions.question: An obese child has dark velvety skin on the back of the neck. What is the underlying problem?
questions.exp: Acanthosis nigricans is a marker of insulin resistance; screen for type 2 diabetes (HbA1c, fasting glucose), dyslipidaemia and fatty liver.

questions.question: A child has a skin infection after varicella. What is the commonest organism?
questions.d: Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) or Staphylococcus aureus
questions.exp: Secondary bacterial infection of chickenpox lesions (cellulitis, necrotising fasciitis, toxic shock) is usually caused by Group A Streptococcus or Staph aureus. Worsening fever after day 3–4 is a red flag.

questions.question: A 2-year-old with high fever and a normal white cell count has Streptococcus pneumoniae in the blood culture after 48 hours. He is still febrile. What should be done?
questions.d: Re-evaluate, repeat the blood culture, consider lumbar puncture and start IV antibiotics
questions.exp: Occult pneumococcal bacteraemia that is still febrile or unwell needs reassessment, repeat cultures, a lumbar puncture if meningitis is possible, and parenteral antibiotics.

questions.question: A child with haemolytic uraemic syndrome has which laboratory finding?
questions.exp: HUS: microangiopathic haemolysis with schistocytes, raised LDH, low haptoglobin, low platelets and acute kidney injury; the Coombs test is negative (except in pneumococcal HUS).

questions.question: A child has a nosebleed. What is the first-aid advice?
questions.a: Pinch the soft part of the nose firmly for 10–15 minutes while leaning forward
questions.b: Apply ice to the back of the neck only
questions.d: Pack the nose with cotton immediately
questions.exp: Most nosebleeds are from Little's area and stop with firm pressure leaning forward; seek help if it continues after 20 minutes, is heavy, or recurs often (look for bleeding disorders).

questions.question: What is suitable empirical treatment for febrile neutropenia?
questions.exp: Give an anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam within 1 hour; add an aminoglycoside if septic, vancomycin for line infection or MRSA risk, and antifungals for persistent fever after 4–7 days.

questions.question: A 4-year-old wets the bed at night but is dry by day and well. What should be done?
questions.exp: Bedwetting is common under 5 years and usually resolves. Treatment (alarm, desmopressin) is considered from about 5–7 years. Check for daytime symptoms, constipation, UTI, diabetes and snoring.

questions.question: A 12-year-old has rectal bleeding, and colonoscopy shows multiple hamartomatous polyps; he has dark pigmented spots on the lips. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Peutz–Jeghers (STK11, autosomal dominant): mucocutaneous pigmentation of lips and mouth with GI hamartomatous polyps causing bleeding and intussusception, and a raised cancer risk. Juvenile polyps without pigmentation are the commonest childhood polyps.

questions.question: A child with Hodgkin lymphoma has involved lymph nodes on both sides of the diaphragm (left cervical, left axillary and mesenteric) with fever. What is the stage?
questions.exp: Ann Arbor staging: I one region, II two or more regions on the same side of the diaphragm, III both sides of the diaphragm, IV extranodal organ involvement (liver, bone marrow, lung). B = fever, night sweats, weight loss over 10%.

questions.question: An infant has vomiting, failure to thrive and dehydration with a hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis and high urinary chloride. His mother had polyhydramnios. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Antenatal or neonatal Bartter syndrome causes polyhydramnios, prematurity, polyuria, dehydration, hypokalaemic alkalosis and hypercalciuria (nephrocalcinosis). In pyloric stenosis, urinary chloride is low.

questions.question: A child with oesophageal varices is bleeding with a low haemoglobin and shock. What is the first priority?
questions.a: Wait for endoscopy before giving any fluid
questions.b: Blood transfusion and resuscitation (with octreotide), then endoscopy
questions.exp: Variceal bleeding: secure the airway, IV access, cautious transfusion to Hb about 7–8 g/dL (overtransfusion raises portal pressure), octreotide, antibiotic prophylaxis, correct coagulopathy, then endoscopic band ligation.

questions.question: Which congenital heart lesion causes oligaemic lung fields on X-ray?
questions.exp: Reduced pulmonary blood flow (oligaemic lungs) with cyanosis: tetralogy of Fallot, pulmonary atresia, tricuspid atresia, Ebstein anomaly. Plethoric lungs with cyanosis: TGA, truncus, TAPVR.

questions.question: A child with nephrotic syndrome on prednisolone 2 mg/kg is cushingoid and has been exposed to a child with chickenpox. He has never had varicella. What should be done?
questions.c: Postpone the vaccine and do nothing else
questions.exp: High-dose steroids make him immunosuppressed: give VZIG within 10 days of exposure (or oral aciclovir from day 7) and treat any chickenpox early with IV aciclovir. Live vaccine is contraindicated.

questions.question: A healthy 4-year-old who had only one dose of varicella vaccine is exposed to chickenpox. What should be done?
questions.a: Give the second dose of varicella vaccine (within 3–5 days of exposure)
questions.exp: Post-exposure varicella vaccine within 3–5 days can prevent or modify disease in healthy children, and the second dose is due anyway.

questions.question: A child can draw a circle and a square, ride a tricycle and name 4 colours. What is the age?
questions.exp: Square and naming colours at about 4 years; circle and tricycle at 3.

questions.question: A breastfed 2-month-old cries for more than 3 hours a day on more than 3 days a week, but examination is normal and he gains weight. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Colic: unexplained crying over 3 hours a day, 3 days a week, in a well thriving infant, peaking at 6 weeks and settling by 3–4 months. Reassure and support the parents; screen for red flags and parental exhaustion.

questions.question: An 8-month-old has bouts of crying for 20 minutes then becomes quiet and lethargic between attacks. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Intussusception: paroxysmal colicky pain with drawing up of legs, lethargy and pallor between episodes, vomiting, then redcurrant jelly stool. Ultrasound confirms; air enema reduces.

questions.question: After a fall, a child cannot move his arms or legs. What imaging is best?
questions.b: MRI of the cervical spine (with CT if bony injury suspected)
questions.exp: Neurological deficits after trauma need MRI of the spine to show cord injury (SCIWORA, spinal cord injury without radiographic abnormality, is more common in children). Immobilise the spine first.

questions.question: A boy hit his head during football, had a lucid interval, then became unconscious. CT shows a biconvex (lens-shaped) haematoma. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Extradural haematoma: usually from middle meningeal artery bleeding with a skull fracture; lens-shaped, does not cross sutures; lucid interval then rapid deterioration. Needs urgent evacuation. Subdural is crescent-shaped and crosses sutures.

questions.question: Which condition can give a falsely POSITIVE sweat test?
questions.c: Adrenal insufficiency (and malnutrition, hypothyroidism, ectodermal dysplasia)
questions.exp: Other causes of false positives: anorexia nervosa, glycogen storage disease type I, mucopolysaccharidoses, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. False negatives occur with oedema and hypoproteinaemia, and insufficient sweat.

questions.question: Where are most encephaloceles located?
questions.exp: About 75% are occipital (linked to Chiari III, Dandy–Walker, Meckel–Gruber syndrome); fronto-ethmoidal encephaloceles are commoner in South East Asia.

questions.question: A child has fever, pancytopenia and hepatosplenomegaly, with more than 20% myeloblasts in the bone marrow. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: AML is diagnosed with 20% or more myeloblasts in the marrow (Auer rods, MPO positive). It is less common than ALL in children (about 15–20% of leukaemias), and more common in Down syndrome (especially M7 under 4 years).

questions.question: A 2-year-old is pale and eats non-food items (pica). What should be checked?
questions.exp: Pica is linked to iron deficiency and lead poisoning (from old paint, some traditional remedies and cosmetics such as kohl). Lead causes microcytic anaemia with basophilic stippling, abdominal pain, behaviour problems and encephalopathy.

questions.question: How long should a child with measles stay off school?
questions.b: Until 4 days after the rash appears
questions.exp: Measles is infectious from about 4 days before to 4 days after the rash starts; exclude from school for 4 days from the onset of the rash.

questions.question: A family member of a kidney transplant recipient needs vaccinations. Which vaccine should NOT be given to household contacts?
questions.exp: Household contacts of immunocompromised people should receive MMR, varicella, rotavirus and inactivated influenza vaccines, but not oral polio vaccine (shed virus can cause vaccine-associated paralytic polio). If a vaccinated contact gets a varicella vaccine rash, avoid close contact.

questions.question: A 2-year-old's weight and length fell from the 50th to below the 3rd centile from 8 months of age. He has poor appetite, hypotonia, delayed walking and a rachitic rosary. What is the investigation?
questions.d: Coeliac serology (anti-tTG IgA with total IgA)
questions.exp: Faltering growth starting after gluten introduction, with irritability, poor appetite, abdominal distension and malabsorption of vitamin D and calcium (rickets), suggests coeliac disease. Also check vitamin D and bone profile.

questions.question: A child drank kerosene and is stable. What should be done?
questions.c: Observe (with chest X-ray at about 6 hours); do not induce vomiting or give charcoal
questions.exp: Hydrocarbons are dangerous mainly through aspiration pneumonitis. Avoid emesis, lavage and charcoal; observe for 6 hours with oxygen saturations and a chest X-ray; discharge if symptomless and X-ray normal.

questions.question: A child had abdominal trauma, recovered and was discharged. Two weeks later he has an epigastric mass and a raised amylase. What should be done?
questions.a: CT of the abdomen (to look for a pseudocyst)
questions.exp: A pancreatic pseudocyst after trauma presents weeks later with a mass and raised enzymes; CT or ultrasound confirms.

questions.question: A child needs surgery for a chest wall deformity (pectus excavatum). What preoperative assessment is needed?
questions.a: Pulmonary function tests and echocardiogram (with chest CT for the Haller index)
questions.exp: Severe pectus excavatum assessment: CT for the Haller index, echo (cardiac compression, mitral valve prolapse, Marfan features) and spirometry.

questions.question: A child with portal hypertension has oesophageal varices, normal blood pressure, low haemoglobin and a high platelet count, with slow bleeding. What drug is used?
questions.exp: Octreotide (somatostatin analogue) reduces portal blood flow and variceal bleeding; give with cautious transfusion, antibiotics and endoscopy. Portal vein thrombosis (normal liver, splenomegaly) is a common cause in children.
